problems.sourceStatement: Show that for polynomially bounded SWCDDM matrices \(M\), Algebraic Multigrid runs in time \(\widetilde O(\operatorname{nnz}(M))\) to compute an implicitly represented symmetric matrix \(Z\), which can be applied in \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(M))\) time, and satisfies \(\Omega(1)M^{-1}\preceq Z\preceq O(1)M^{-1}\). In particular, the constants are independent of the problem size \(n\).
problems.problem: Prove a near-linear construction and linear-time application guarantee for an algebraic-multigrid approximate inverse of every polynomially bounded SWCDDM matrix.
problems.wordDescription: Algebraic multigrid is among the most successful practical methods for elliptic and graph-structured systems, but a theorem matching its observed near-linear behavior on this broad matrix class is missing. The requested result would translate multigrid hierarchies into the spectral-approximation language common in theoretical computer science. It would also clarify whether purely algebraic coarsening can achieve the same kind of nearly linear guarantee as specialized Laplacian solvers.
problems.mathematicalConditions: For every polynomially bounded symmetric weakly chained diagonally dominant M-matrix \(M\), compute an implicit symmetric operator \(Z\) in \(\widetilde O(\operatorname{nnz}(M))\) time such that \(Z\) is a constant-factor Loewner approximation to \(M^{-1}\). Applying \(Z\) to a vector must cost \(O(\operatorname{nnz}(M))\), with approximation constants independent of \(n\). The paper also highlights planar-only and mildly relaxed construction/application variants.

problems.sourceStatement: Fix constants \(\varepsilon>0\) and \(p>0\). Let \(A_n=U\Lambda_nU^*\), where \(U\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}\) is Haar unitary and \(\Lambda_n=\operatorname{diag}(1^{-p},2^{-p},\ldots,n^{-p})\). Let \(b_n=A_nz_n\), where \(z_n\) is distributed uniformly on the sphere. What is the asymptotic behavior of \(T_{\mathrm{CG}}(A_n,b_n,\varepsilon)\) compared with \(T_{\mathrm{RCD}}(A_n,b_n,\varepsilon)\) as \(n\to\infty\)?
problems.problem: Determine the asymptotic iteration complexity of conjugate gradients versus randomized coordinate descent on random-basis systems with polynomially decaying eigenvalues.
problems.wordDescription: Worst-case condition numbers do not capture how iterative methods exploit a full eigenvalue distribution. This model fixes a controlled power-law spectrum, randomizes the eigenbasis, and chooses a generic solution direction. It therefore offers a clean test of whether Krylov polynomial approximation or coordinate sampling better exploits spectral decay. A sharp answer could reveal distribution-sensitive complexity measures that are more predictive than the ordinary condition number.
problems.mathematicalConditions: For fixed \(p,\varepsilon>0\), characterize with high probability or in expectation the growth rates in \(n\) of the stopping times for CG and RCD applied to the stated random system. The stopping criterion should be the paper's prescribed relative error measure. Determine the ratio or asymptotic ordering of the two complexities, including any phase transitions as a function of \(p\).

problems.sourceStatement: Find the smallest \(p>0\) such that we can solve an \(n\times n\) linear system \(Ax=b\) to high accuracy using \(\widetilde O(T_A\,\bar\kappa_p)\) arithmetic operations, where \(\bar\kappa_p\) is the \(p\)-averaged condition number of the singular values of \(A\), whereas \(T_A\) is either \(n^2\) or \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\).
problems.problem: Determine the strongest averaged-condition-number dependence achievable by fast dense and sparse linear-system solvers.
problems.wordDescription: The ordinary condition number is controlled by the single smallest singular value, even when almost all singular values are benign. Averaged condition numbers interpolate between a bulk statistic and the worst case. The problem asks how far solver complexity can be made sensitive to this average and whether sparse access creates a fundamental barrier that is absent in dense systems.
problems.mathematicalConditions: For singular values \(\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_n>0\), let \(\bar\kappa_p=(n^{-1}\sum_i(\sigma_i/\sigma_n)^p)^{1/p}\). Find the infimum of \(p>0\) for which every input can be solved to high accuracy in \(\widetilde O(T_A\bar\kappa_p)\) operations, separately for \(T_A=n^2\) and \(T_A=\operatorname{nnz}(A)\), or prove lower bounds ruling out such dependence.

comments.body:
**Freshness update (checked 2026-08-09).**

- [Conditional Hardness for Averaged-Condition Linear-System Solvers](https://yangpliu.github.io/repo/averaged-condition-hardness/paper.pdf) (July 31, 2026; manuscript; no conventional author is listed). The paper says it was fully AI-generated by a GPT 5.6 Sol Ultra harness from a prompt based on observations by Junzhao Yang. Assuming a dense optimality hypothesis for condition number $\kappa=n^\alpha$, it uses identity padding to derive conditional lower bounds for the two access models in Problem 2.6. For sparse access, it rules out $\widetilde O(\operatorname{nnz}(A) \bar\kappa_p(A))$ below an explicit $\alpha$-dependent threshold, and rules out every fixed finite $p$ if the hypothesis holds for arbitrarily small positive $\alpha$. For dense access, it rules out $\widetilde O(N^2\bar\kappa_p(A))$ for $p<1/4$ in the mildly conditioned regime. The boundary cases are not claimed, and the dense $p<1/4$ barrier is specific to the identity-padding reduction.

**Problem status: open, with conditional lower-bound progress.** The paper sharply constrains the possible averaged-condition dependence under its stated hypothesis, but it neither proves an unconditional lower bound nor determines the smallest feasible $p$ in the remaining dense regime. Its theorem is stated in bit complexity, whereas the Simons source asks for arithmetic-operation complexity, so this model difference is another reason not to mark the problem solved.

problems.sourceStatement: Let \(A\) be an \(n\times n\) random matrix with i.i.d. Gaussian (or Rademacher, or Bernoulli) entries, and take any \(n\)-dimensional vector \(b\). Is it possible, conditioned on a high-probability event, to solve \(Ax=b\) to high accuracy faster than \(O(n^\omega)\)?
problems.problem: Solve a typical i.i.d. random dense linear system asymptotically faster than general matrix inversion, for an arbitrary right-hand side.
problems.wordDescription: Random dense matrices are usually well behaved in many senses, yet the smallest singular values still create nontrivial inverse complexity. The question asks whether typical-case structure can beat the matrix-multiplication barrier, even when the right-hand side is adversarial. A positive result would be a strong example of an average-case speedup for a fundamental algebraic problem.
problems.mathematicalConditions: For \(A\) drawn from an i.i.d. Gaussian, Rademacher, or Bernoulli ensemble, construct an algorithm that, on an event of probability \(1-o(1)\) over \(A\), solves \(Ax=b\) for every fixed or arbitrary \(b\) to high accuracy in \(o(n^\omega)\) time. Alternatively, prove a matching conditional or oracle lower bound. Matrix-vector complexity variants are also relevant.

problems.sourceStatement: Prove the Forsythe conjecture: for every restart length \(2\le s<d(A)\), each of the two normalized-residual subsequences \(\{y_{2k}\}\) and \(\{y_{2k+1}\}\) generated by exact conjugate gradients restarted every \(s\) steps has a single limit vector.
problems.problem: Prove parity-subsequence convergence of normalized residual directions for exact conjugate gradients restarted every \(s\) steps, for all \(2\le s<d(A)\).
problems.wordDescription: Forsythe's optimum \(s\)-gradient method is, in modern terms, conjugate gradients restarted every \(s\) steps. Forsythe proved the two-cycle limiting-direction result for \(s=1\), where the method is mathematically equivalent to steepest descent, and conjectured the same parity convergence for every fixed restart length. The question concerns existence of the two limit directions rather than the convergence rate. If the conjecture holds, residuals of each parity become asymptotically collinear, so the restarted iteration can converge at best linearly in the limit.
problems.mathematicalConditions: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive definite, let \(b\in\mathbb R^n\), and let \(x=A^{-1}b\). Fix an integer \(2\le s<d(A)\), where \(d(A)\) is the degree of the minimal polynomial of \(A\), and assume \(d(A,r_0)\ge s+1\) for \(r_0=b-Ax_0\). For \(k=0,1,2,\ldots\), set \(y_k=r_k/\|r_k\|\), where \(r_k=b-Ax_k\), and choose \(x_{k+1}\in x_k+\mathcal K_s(A,y_k)\) so that \(x-x_{k+1}\perp_A\mathcal K_s(A,y_k)\), with \(\mathcal K_s(A,y_k)=\operatorname{span}\{y_k,Ay_k,\ldots,A^{s-1}y_k\}\). Prove that each of \(\{y_{2k}\}\) and \(\{y_{2k+1}\}\) has a single limit vector.

comments.body:
**Freshness update (searched through 2026-08-08).**

Three proof manuscripts for the case s=2 appeared within a few days:

- [A Proof of the Forsythe Conjecture for the Two-Step Restarted Conjugate Gradient Method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.02852) — Matthew J. Colbrook, George Stepaniants, and Alex Townsend (2026). This arXiv preprint proves that, unless the iteration terminates, the even and odd normalized residual subsequences converge separately.
- [Proof of the Forsythe Conjecture for s = 2](https://jarek.ai/papers/proof-of-the-forsythe-conjecture-for-s-2.pdf) — Jarek Liesen (2026). It gives a proof through the monic degree-two Arnoldi iteration and applies to real symmetric matrices, hence covers the positive-definite setting. The manuscript states that expert review is still in progress and acknowledges a minor inaccuracy in the equation following (10).
- [Convergence of Normalized Residuals for Restarted Conjugate Gradients of Length Two](https://yangpliu.github.io/repo/restarted-cg-two/paper.pdf) (2026). This manuscript proves the exact SPD restarted-CG result without a simple-spectrum or genericity assumption. It states that it was fully AI-generated by a GPT-5.6-Sol Ultra harness from a one-shot prompt by Richard Peng and does not list a conventional author.

**Problem status: partially solved relative to the source problem. The case s=2 is now resolved with substantially stronger corroboration from three near-simultaneous proof manuscripts; restart lengths s>=3 remain open. These are three proof manuscripts/preprints, not three peer-reviewed publications.**

**Source note:** Simons Problem 2.20 asks for every 2<=s<d(A); the corrected JSON body and the status above follow that formulation.

Several people have tried to find a proof for the case s=2 using ChatGPT over the last few months. Attempts failed until very recently, when three proofs for this case using GPT-5.6 appeared in a short timeframe:

**Freshness update (searched through 2026-08-06).**

It proves that every real degree-eight polynomial of exact degree eight can be evaluated with three matrix-matrix multiplications, constructs recursive step/sign approximants in this enlarged class, and reports consistent multiplication-count reductions.

**Problem status: open, with constructive partial progress.** The paper supplies new upper constructions but explicitly leaves optimal polynomial sequences open and gives neither the requested global asymptotics nor matching lower bounds.

**Review flag:** the result is directly multiplication-budget-aware, but it studies a recursive component class rather than optimizing over all of Pi_m^*.
